facts.fact_text: On 6 May 2012 a public demonstration entitled the 'March of Millions' was held in central Moscow.
The 'March of Millions' demonstration on 6 May 2012 was held to protest against the allegedly rigged presidential elections.
The 'March of Millions' demonstration on 6 May 2012 had been approved by the Moscow city authorities in the form of a march followed by a meeting at Bolotnaya Square.
The approved demonstration on 6 May 2012 was supposed to end at 7.30 p.m.
The march on 6 May 2012 was peaceful and held without any disruptions.
When the marchers arrived at Bolotnaya Square on 6 May 2012, it became apparent that barriers installed by the police had narrowed the entrance to the meeting venue.
The barriers installed by the police at Bolotnaya Square on 6 May 2012 allegedly restricted the space allocated for the meeting.
To control the crowd at Bolotnaya Square on 6 May 2012, a police cordon forced the protestors to remain within the barriers.
There were numerous clashes between the police and protesters at Bolotnaya Square on 6 May 2012.
At 5.30 p.m. on 6 May 2012 the police ordered that the meeting at Bolotnaya Square finish early.
At 5.30 p.m. on 6 May 2012 the police began to disperse the participants of the demonstration at Bolotnaya Square.
It took the police about two hours to clear the protestors from Bolotnaya Square on 6 May 2012.
The first applicant (Mr Aristov) and the second applicant (Mr Gromov) took part in the demonstration on 6 May 2012 at Bolotnaya Square.
When the marchers arrived at Bolotnaya Square on 6 May 2012, it became apparent that barriers installed by the police had narrowed the entrance to the meeting venue.
The barriers installed by the police at Bolotnaya Square on 6 May 2012 allegedly restricted the space allocated for the meeting.
To control the crowd at Bolotnaya Square on 6 May 2012, a police cordon forced the protestors to remain within the barriers.
There were numerous clashes between the police and protesters at Bolotnaya Square on 6 May 2012.
At 5.30 p.m. on 6 May 2012 the police ordered that the meeting at Bolotnaya Square finish early.
At 5.30 p.m. on 6 May 2012 the police began to disperse the participants of the demonstration at Bolotnaya Square.
It took the police about two hours to clear the protestors from Bolotnaya Square on 6 May 2012.
The first applicant (Mr Aristov) and the second applicant (Mr Gromov) were arrested at the venue of the demonstration on 6 May 2012.
According to the first applicant (Mr Aristov), at 6 p.m. on 6 May 2012 he was picked out of the crowd and apprehended by the police.
According to the Government, the first applicant (Mr Aristov) was arrested at 6 p.m. on 6 May 2012 at Bolotnaya Square.
According to the Government, the first applicant (Mr Aristov) was arrested because he had participated in breaking the police cordon at Bolotnaya Square on 6 May 2012.
According to the Government, the first applicant (Mr Aristov) was arrested because he had disregarded police orders to cease his actions at Bolotnaya Square on 6 May 2012.
At 7.20 p.m. on 6 May 2012 the first applicant (Mr Aristov) was brought to Basmannyy district police station in Moscow.
At Basmannyy district police station, an on-duty officer drew up a record of the first applicant's (Mr Aristov's) administrative escort for the purpose of compiling an administrative file.
The record of administrative arrest of the first applicant (Mr Aristov) indicated that he had been arrested at 7.20 p.m. at Basmannyy district police station.
The record of administrative arrest of the first applicant (Mr Aristov) indicated that he was released on 7 May 2012 at 9.20 a.m.

An on-duty officer at Basmannyy district police station drew up an administrative-offence record against the first applicant (Mr Aristov) on the basis of reports and explanatory notes by police officers P. and Ch., who had arrested the applicant.
The reports and explanatory notes by police officers P. and Ch. regarding the first applicant (Mr Aristov) were drawn up using an identical template.

The reports and explanatory notes by police officers P. and Ch. regarding the first applicant (Mr Aristov) contained no individualised information except the police officers' personal information and the applicant's name.
The first applicant (Mr Aristov) was accused of having disobeyed a lawful order of the police, an offence under Article 19.3 § 1 of the Code of Administrative Offences.

The administrative-offence record against the first applicant (Mr Aristov) reiterated the police reports, stating that the applicant, acting as part of a group of 15,000 citizens, took part in an authorised meeting.

The administrative-offence record against the first applicant (Mr Aristov) stated that the applicant chanted slogans 'Russia without Putin', 'Putin is a thief', and 'United Russia is a party of crooks and thieves'.
The administrative-offence record against the first applicant (Mr Aristov) stated that during the event the participants broke the police cordon and tried to enter Red Square.

The administrative-offence record against the first applicant (Mr Aristov) stated that the applicant did not react to the multiple lawful demands of Officers P. and Ch. to stop breaking the police cordon and continued his unlawful acts, in breach of Article 19.3 § 1 of the Code of Administrative Offences.
On 7 May 2012 the first applicant (Mr Aristov) was brought before the Justice of the Peace of Court Circuit no. 100 of the Yakimanka District of Moscow.

Before the Justice of the Peace of Court Circuit no. 100 of the Yakimanka District of Moscow, the first applicant (Mr Aristov) insisted that he had not broken the police cordon and had been arrested by the police with no warnings or orders.

The first applicant (Mr Aristov) applied to have the two police officers who had arrested him examined as witnesses before the Justice of the Peace of Court Circuit no. 100 of the Yakimanka District of Moscow.

The Justice of the Peace of Court Circuit no. 100 of the Yakimanka District of Moscow rejected the first applicant's (Mr Aristov's) application to have the two arresting police officers examined as witnesses, in order to expedite the proceedings.
The Justice of the Peace of Court Circuit no. 100 of the Yakimanka District of Moscow questioned two witnesses for the defence in the case of the first applicant (Mr Aristov).
The Justice of the Peace of Court Circuit no. 100 of the Yakimanka District of Moscow examined a video recording submitted by the first applicant's (Mr Aristov's) representative.

On the basis of the police officers' reports and explanations and the records of the administrative escorting and arrest, the Justice of the Peace of Court Circuit no. 100 of the Yakimanka District of Moscow established that the first applicant (Mr Aristov) had committed an administrative offence under Article 19.3 § 1 of the Code of Administrative Offences, as described in the administrative-offence record.

The Justice of the Peace of Court Circuit no. 100 of the Yakimanka District of Moscow dismissed as unreliable the testimony of defence witnesses, who stated that the first applicant (Mr Aristov) had not chanted any slogans in their presence and had not participated in breaking the cordon.

The Justice of the Peace of Court Circuit no. 100 of the Yakimanka District of Moscow dismissed the video recording submitted by the first applicant (Mr Aristov) on the grounds that it showed the background of the events in question rather than the applicant's arrest.

The Justice of the Peace of Court Circuit no. 100 of the Yakimanka District of Moscow dismissed the video recording submitted by the first applicant (Mr Aristov) on the additional grounds that it did not contain any sound and could not therefore prove whether the applicant had chanted any slogans or not.
The Justice of the Peace of Court Circuit no. 100 of the Yakimanka District of Moscow sentenced the first applicant (Mr Aristov) to twenty-four hours' administrative detention.
On 22 May 2012 the Zamoskvoretskiy District Court of Moscow examined the first applicant's (Mr Aristov's) appeal against the judgment of 7 May 2012.
Before the Zamoskvoretskiy District Court of Moscow, the first applicant (Mr Aristov) repeated his application to summon and question the two police officers who had arrested him on 6 May 2012.

The Zamoskvoretskiy District Court of Moscow rejected the first applicant's (Mr Aristov's) application to summon and question the two arresting police officers owing to the applicant's failure to name those officers.
Before the Zamoskvoretskiy District Court of Moscow, the first applicant (Mr Aristov) insisted that he had not chanted any slogans and had not participated in breaking the police cordon.
The Zamoskvoretskiy District Court of Moscow questioned two defence witnesses who confirmed the first applicant's (Mr Aristov's) account of events but stated that they had not observed his arrest.
The Zamoskvoretskiy District Court of Moscow dismissed the testimony of the two defence witnesses as unreliable because both witnesses were the first applicant's (Mr Aristov's) friends.

Relying on the reports and written statements of the police officers, the Zamoskvoretskiy District Court of Moscow upheld the first-instance judgment convicting the first applicant (Mr Aristov) of an administrative offence under Article 19.3 § 1 of the Code of Administrative Offences.
According to the second applicant (Mr Gromov), on 6 May 2012 at 4 p.m. he came to Bolotnaya Square to participate in the authorised demonstration.
According to the second applicant (Mr Gromov), he could not leave the venue of the demonstration on 6 May 2012 because all the ways out of Bolotnaya Square had been cordoned off by the police.
According to the second applicant (Mr Gromov), he stood in the crowd at Bolotnaya Square waiting for further information about the demonstration from its organisers.

According to the second applicant (Mr Gromov), around 7.30 p.m. on 6 May 2012 he saw State Duma Deputy Ponomarev with a megaphone and came closer to listen to him together with ten other participants.

According to the second applicant (Mr Gromov), at that moment a few police officers ran out of the cordon and arrested State Duma Deputy Ponomarev and everyone around him, including the second applicant (Mr Gromov).
According to the Government, the second applicant (Mr Gromov) was arrested at 8.10 p.m. on 6 May 2012 at Bolotnaya Square.
According to the Government, the second applicant (Mr Gromov) was arrested because he was participating in breaking the police cordon at Bolotnaya Square on 6 May 2012.
According to the Government, the second applicant (Mr Gromov) was arrested because he had disregarded the police order to cease breaking the police cordon and to disperse.
At 9 p.m. on 6 May 2012 the second applicant (Mr Gromov) was brought to Veshnyaki district police station in Moscow.

At Veshnyaki district police station, an on-duty officer drew up a record of the second applicant's (Mr Gromov's) administrative escort at 9.10 p.m. on 6 May 2012 for the purpose of compiling an administrative-offence record.
At 9.20 p.m. on 6 May 2012 the second applicant (Mr Gromov) was administratively arrested at Veshnyaki district police station.
According to the record of the second applicant's (Mr Gromov's) administrative arrest, he was released on 7 May 2012 at 10.50 a.m.
The second applicant (Mr Gromov) was accused of having disobeyed a lawful order of the police, an offence under Article 19.3 § 1 of the Code of Administrative Offences.

The administrative-offence record against the second applicant (Mr Gromov) contained a printed template stating that the police repeatedly announced through a loudhailer lawful demands to stop the march but the applicant, acting as part of a group of citizens, broke the police cordon.

The administrative-offence record against the second applicant (Mr Gromov) stated that the applicant did not react to multiple demands to cease these actions and disperse, and continued his unlawful acts, thereby attracting the attention of the public and mass media.

The administrative-offence record against the second applicant (Mr Gromov) stated that the applicant tried to cause confusion among the public (создать суматоху среди граждан), thereby demonstrating his refusal to obey the lawful orders of the police officers and precluding them from fulfilling their service duties, in breach of Article 19.3 § 1 of the Code of Administrative Offences.
The administrative case file of the second applicant (Mr Gromov) contained two hand-written reports by police officers D. and S., who had arrested the second applicant on 6 May 2012.
The hand-written reports by police officers D. and S. repeated the description of the second applicant's (Mr Gromov's) acts contained in the administrative-offence record.
On 7 May 2012 the second applicant (Mr Gromov) was brought before the Justice of the Peace of Court Circuit no. 100 of the Yakimanka District of Moscow.
The Justice of the Peace of Court Circuit no. 100 of the Yakimanka District of Moscow adjourned the case of the second applicant (Mr Gromov) to 17 May 2012.

On 15 May 2012 the Justice of the Peace of Court Circuit no. 100 of the Yakimanka District of Moscow decided to transfer the case of the second applicant (Mr Gromov) owing to the lack of jurisdiction.
On 14 August 2012 the Justice of the Peace of Court Circuit no. 114 of the Luberetskiy Court District of Moscow Region examined the charges against the second applicant (Mr Gromov).

Upon the second applicant's (Mr Gromov's) application, the Justice of the Peace of Court Circuit no. 114 of the Luberetskiy Court District of Moscow Region questioned the applicant's sister, who was an eyewitness to his arrest.

The second applicant's (Mr Gromov's) sister confirmed his account of events — that he had come closer to listen to State Duma Deputy Ponomarev and was arrested along with those around the deputy — but the Justice of the Peace of Court Circuit no. 114 of the Luberetskiy Court District of Moscow Region dismissed her statements as unreliable evidence.

The Justice of the Peace of Court Circuit no. 114 of the Luberetskiy Court District of Moscow Region questioned Officers D. and S., who stated that after the end of the demonstration, at around 8 p.m. on 6 May 2012, the second applicant (Mr Gromov), acting as part of a group of citizens, had broken the police cordon and begun the march towards Red Square.

Officers D. and S. stated that as the second applicant (Mr Gromov) had not reacted to multiple demands to stop, he had been arrested together with other participants following a radio communication order.

On the basis of the police officers' statements and reports, the Justice of the Peace of Court Circuit no. 114 of the Luberetskiy Court District of Moscow Region found the second applicant (Mr Gromov) guilty under Article 19.3 § 1 of the Code of Administrative Offences.

The Justice of the Peace of Court Circuit no. 114 of the Luberetskiy Court District of Moscow Region sentenced the second applicant (Mr Gromov) to a fine of 700 Russian roubles (approximately 18 euros at the time).
The second applicant (Mr Gromov) appealed against the judgment of 14 August 2012, pointing out that he had been arrested by riot squad officers rather than by Officers D. and S.
On 24 September 2012 the Lyuberetskiy Town Court of the Moscow Region examined the second applicant's (Mr Gromov's) appeal against the judgment of 14 August 2012.
The Lyuberetskiy Town Court of the Moscow Region upheld the judgment of 14 August 2012 convicting the second applicant (Mr Gromov) under Article 19.3 § 1 of the Code of Administrative Offences.
The Lyuberetskiy Town Court of the Moscow Region dismissed the second applicant's (Mr Gromov's) allegations that he had been arrested by riot squad officers rather than by Officers D. and S.

The Lyuberetskiy Town Court of the Moscow Region considered that the statements of Officers D. and S. about the second applicant's (Mr Gromov's) failure to obey their lawful demands to stop marching after the end of the event had been trustworthy.

The record of administrative arrest of the first applicant (Mr Aristov) indicated that he had been arrested at 7.20 p.m. at Basmannyy district police station.
The record of administrative arrest of the first applicant (Mr Aristov) indicated that he was released on 7 May 2012 at 9.20 a.m.

An on-duty officer at Basmannyy district police station drew up an administrative-offence record against the first applicant (Mr Aristov) on the basis of reports and explanatory notes by police officers P. and Ch., who had arrested the applicant.
The reports and explanatory notes by police officers P. and Ch. regarding the first applicant (Mr Aristov) were drawn up using an identical template.

The reports and explanatory notes by police officers P. and Ch. regarding the first applicant (Mr Aristov) contained no individualised information except the police officers' personal information and the applicant's name.
The first applicant (Mr Aristov) was accused of having disobeyed a lawful order of the police, an offence under Article 19.3 § 1 of the Code of Administrative Offences.

The administrative-offence record against the first applicant (Mr Aristov) reiterated the police reports, stating that the applicant, acting as part of a group of 15,000 citizens, took part in an authorised meeting.

The administrative-offence record against the first applicant (Mr Aristov) stated that the applicant chanted slogans 'Russia without Putin', 'Putin is a thief', and 'United Russia is a party of crooks and thieves'.
The administrative-offence record against the first applicant (Mr Aristov) stated that during the event the participants broke the police cordon and tried to enter Red Square.

The administrative-offence record against the first applicant (Mr Aristov) stated that the applicant did not react to the multiple lawful demands of Officers P. and Ch. to stop breaking the police cordon and continued his unlawful acts, in breach of Article 19.3 § 1 of the Code of Administrative Offences.
On 7 May 2012 the first applicant (Mr Aristov) was brought before the Justice of the Peace of Court Circuit no. 100 of the Yakimanka District of Moscow.

Before the Justice of the Peace of Court Circuit no. 100 of the Yakimanka District of Moscow, the first applicant (Mr Aristov) insisted that he had not broken the police cordon and had been arrested by the police with no warnings or orders.

The first applicant (Mr Aristov) applied to have the two police officers who had arrested him examined as witnesses before the Justice of the Peace of Court Circuit no. 100 of the Yakimanka District of Moscow.

The Justice of the Peace of Court Circuit no. 100 of the Yakimanka District of Moscow rejected the first applicant's (Mr Aristov's) application to have the two arresting police officers examined as witnesses, in order to expedite the proceedings.
The Justice of the Peace of Court Circuit no. 100 of the Yakimanka District of Moscow questioned two witnesses for the defence in the case of the first applicant (Mr Aristov).
The Justice of the Peace of Court Circuit no. 100 of the Yakimanka District of Moscow examined a video recording submitted by the first applicant's (Mr Aristov's) representative.

On the basis of the police officers' reports and explanations and the records of the administrative escorting and arrest, the Justice of the Peace of Court Circuit no. 100 of the Yakimanka District of Moscow established that the first applicant (Mr Aristov) had committed an administrative offence under Article 19.3 § 1 of the Code of Administrative Offences, as described in the administrative-offence record.

The Justice of the Peace of Court Circuit no. 100 of the Yakimanka District of Moscow dismissed as unreliable the testimony of defence witnesses, who stated that the first applicant (Mr Aristov) had not chanted any slogans in their presence and had not participated in breaking the cordon.

The Justice of the Peace of Court Circuit no. 100 of the Yakimanka District of Moscow dismissed the video recording submitted by the first applicant (Mr Aristov) on the grounds that it showed the background of the events in question rather than the applicant's arrest.

The Justice of the Peace of Court Circuit no. 100 of the Yakimanka District of Moscow dismissed the video recording submitted by the first applicant (Mr Aristov) on the additional grounds that it did not contain any sound and could not therefore prove whether the applicant had chanted any slogans or not.
The Justice of the Peace of Court Circuit no. 100 of the Yakimanka District of Moscow sentenced the first applicant (Mr Aristov) to twenty-four hours' administrative detention.
On 22 May 2012 the Zamoskvoretskiy District Court of Moscow examined the first applicant's (Mr Aristov's) appeal against the judgment of 7 May 2012.
Before the Zamoskvoretskiy District Court of Moscow, the first applicant (Mr Aristov) repeated his application to summon and question the two police officers who had arrested him on 6 May 2012.

The Zamoskvoretskiy District Court of Moscow rejected the first applicant's (Mr Aristov's) application to summon and question the two arresting police officers owing to the applicant's failure to name those officers.
Before the Zamoskvoretskiy District Court of Moscow, the first applicant (Mr Aristov) insisted that he had not chanted any slogans and had not participated in breaking the police cordon.
The Zamoskvoretskiy District Court of Moscow questioned two defence witnesses who confirmed the first applicant's (Mr Aristov's) account of events but stated that they had not observed his arrest.
The Zamoskvoretskiy District Court of Moscow dismissed the testimony of the two defence witnesses as unreliable because both witnesses were the first applicant's (Mr Aristov's) friends.

Relying on the reports and written statements of the police officers, the Zamoskvoretskiy District Court of Moscow upheld the first-instance judgment convicting the first applicant (Mr Aristov) of an administrative offence under Article 19.3 § 1 of the Code of Administrative Offences.
According to the second applicant (Mr Gromov), on 6 May 2012 at 4 p.m. he came to Bolotnaya Square to participate in the authorised demonstration.
According to the second applicant (Mr Gromov), he could not leave the venue of the demonstration on 6 May 2012 because all the ways out of Bolotnaya Square had been cordoned off by the police.
According to the second applicant (Mr Gromov), he stood in the crowd at Bolotnaya Square waiting for further information about the demonstration from its organisers.

According to the second applicant (Mr Gromov), around 7.30 p.m. on 6 May 2012 he saw State Duma Deputy Ponomarev with a megaphone and came closer to listen to him together with ten other participants.

According to the second applicant (Mr Gromov), at that moment a few police officers ran out of the cordon and arrested State Duma Deputy Ponomarev and everyone around him, including the second applicant (Mr Gromov).
According to the Government, the second applicant (Mr Gromov) was arrested at 8.10 p.m. on 6 May 2012 at Bolotnaya Square.
According to the Government, the second applicant (Mr Gromov) was arrested because he was participating in breaking the police cordon at Bolotnaya Square on 6 May 2012.
According to the Government, the second applicant (Mr Gromov) was arrested because he had disregarded the police order to cease breaking the police cordon and to disperse.
At 9 p.m. on 6 May 2012 the second applicant (Mr Gromov) was brought to Veshnyaki district police station in Moscow.

At Veshnyaki district police station, an on-duty officer drew up a record of the second applicant's (Mr Gromov's) administrative escort at 9.10 p.m. on 6 May 2012 for the purpose of compiling an administrative-offence record.
At 9.20 p.m. on 6 May 2012 the second applicant (Mr Gromov) was administratively arrested at Veshnyaki district police station.
According to the record of the second applicant's (Mr Gromov's) administrative arrest, he was released on 7 May 2012 at 10.50 a.m.
The second applicant (Mr Gromov) was accused of having disobeyed a lawful order of the police, an offence under Article 19.3 § 1 of the Code of Administrative Offences.

The administrative-offence record against the second applicant (Mr Gromov) contained a printed template stating that the police repeatedly announced through a loudhailer lawful demands to stop the march but the applicant, acting as part of a group of citizens, broke the police cordon.

The administrative-offence record against the second applicant (Mr Gromov) stated that the applicant did not react to multiple demands to cease these actions and disperse, and continued his unlawful acts, thereby attracting the attention of the public and mass media.

The administrative-offence record against the second applicant (Mr Gromov) stated that the applicant tried to cause confusion among the public (создать суматоху среди граждан), thereby demonstrating his refusal to obey the lawful orders of the police officers and precluding them from fulfilling their service duties, in breach of Article 19.3 § 1 of the Code of Administrative Offences.
The administrative case file of the second applicant (Mr Gromov) contained two hand-written reports by police officers D. and S., who had arrested the second applicant on 6 May 2012.
The hand-written reports by police officers D. and S. repeated the description of the second applicant's (Mr Gromov's) acts contained in the administrative-offence record.
On 7 May 2012 the second applicant (Mr Gromov) was brought before the Justice of the Peace of Court Circuit no. 100 of the Yakimanka District of Moscow.
The Justice of the Peace of Court Circuit no. 100 of the Yakimanka District of Moscow adjourned the case of the second applicant (Mr Gromov) to 17 May 2012.

On 15 May 2012 the Justice of the Peace of Court Circuit no. 100 of the Yakimanka District of Moscow decided to transfer the case of the second applicant (Mr Gromov) owing to the lack of jurisdiction.
On 14 August 2012 the Justice of the Peace of Court Circuit no. 114 of the Luberetskiy Court District of Moscow Region examined the charges against the second applicant (Mr Gromov).

Upon the second applicant's (Mr Gromov's) application, the Justice of the Peace of Court Circuit no. 114 of the Luberetskiy Court District of Moscow Region questioned the applicant's sister, who was an eyewitness to his arrest.

The second applicant's (Mr Gromov's) sister confirmed his account of events — that he had come closer to listen to State Duma Deputy Ponomarev and was arrested along with those around the deputy — but the Justice of the Peace of Court Circuit no. 114 of the Luberetskiy Court District of Moscow Region dismissed her statements as unreliable evidence.

The Justice of the Peace of Court Circuit no. 114 of the Luberetskiy Court District of Moscow Region questioned Officers D. and S., who stated that after the end of the demonstration, at around 8 p.m. on 6 May 2012, the second applicant (Mr Gromov), acting as part of a group of citizens, had broken the police cordon and begun the march towards Red Square.

Officers D. and S. stated that as the second applicant (Mr Gromov) had not reacted to multiple demands to stop, he had been arrested together with other participants following a radio communication order.

On the basis of the police officers' statements and reports, the Justice of the Peace of Court Circuit no. 114 of the Luberetskiy Court District of Moscow Region found the second applicant (Mr Gromov) guilty under Article 19.3 § 1 of the Code of Administrative Offences.

The Justice of the Peace of Court Circuit no. 114 of the Luberetskiy Court District of Moscow Region sentenced the second applicant (Mr Gromov) to a fine of 700 Russian roubles (approximately 18 euros at the time).
The second applicant (Mr Gromov) appealed against the judgment of 14 August 2012, pointing out that he had been arrested by riot squad officers rather than by Officers D. and S.
On 24 September 2012 the Lyuberetskiy Town Court of the Moscow Region examined the second applicant's (Mr Gromov's) appeal against the judgment of 14 August 2012.
The Lyuberetskiy Town Court of the Moscow Region upheld the judgment of 14 August 2012 convicting the second applicant (Mr Gromov) under Article 19.3 § 1 of the Code of Administrative Offences.
The Lyuberetskiy Town Court of the Moscow Region dismissed the second applicant's (Mr Gromov's) allegations that he had been arrested by riot squad officers rather than by Officers D. and S.

The Lyuberetskiy Town Court of the Moscow Region considered that the statements of Officers D. and S. about the second applicant's (Mr Gromov's) failure to obey their lawful demands to stop marching after the end of the event had been trustworthy.
For a summary of the relevant domestic law applicable to the present cases, see Frumkin v. Russia (no. 74568/12, §§ 77-79, 5 January 2016).
